notes: Adversarial suite of five synthetic deals, each planting one or two rows of the SKILL.md trap map (Where Mistakes Hide) in the user's own request, so that a skill that follows the user literally fails. Rows targeted: newest agreement draft and agreement definitions including party scope (eval 1), data room and executed-contract substance (eval 2), the 'reasonably apparent on its face' cross-reference clause (eval 3), schedule supplements and New York buyer-knowledge law (eval 4), and litigation files with counsel's advice plus knowledge qualifiers (eval 5). No eval expects output that a SKILL.md hard stop would block: every prompt supplies the operative agreement text, and none asks for a misstated fact. No Must line depends on a fact marked [VERIFY] in references/primary-sources.md; the privilege-waiver Must in eval 5 requires both readings. Readiness labels are quoted from references/output-template.md. Key figures recomputed by script on 2026-10-30: eval 1 annualized amounts 264,000 / 240,000 / 280,000 / 234,000 against a 250,000 threshold; eval 2 unreviewed documents 412 - 160 = 252 and Halvorsen share 3.1 / 14.2 = 21.8%; eval 4 deductible 600,000, cap 6,000,000, maximum recovery 1,200,000 on a 1,800,000 claim. All companies and people are fictional. Today's date in every prompt is October 30, 2026.

evals.name: renumbered-reps-and-material-contract-population
evals.prompt: Today is Friday, October 30, 2026. We represent Harbor Holdings Inc., which is selling all of the stock of Pinecrest Packaging Co., a Delaware corporation, to Talon Industrial Partners LLC under a Stock Purchase Agreement governed by Delaware law. Please update our disclosure schedules for signing next week. Our schedules were built on SPA draft 4 (October 8, 2026): Schedule 3.9 (Litigation) lists two pending lawsuits; Schedule 3.11(b) (Leased Real Property) lists the Kessler Road warehouse lease between Pinecrest and Kessler Properties LLC at $19,500 per month; Schedule 3.12(a) (Material Contracts) lists the Brightline Freight master services agreement at $22,000 per month, the Corvane Software license at $240,000 per year, and the Delmar Logistics warehousing agreement at $410,000 per year. Buyer's counsel circulated SPA draft 5 on October 22, 2026. It inserts a new Section 3.9 (Environmental Matters), so Litigation is now Section 3.10, Compliance with Laws 3.11, Real Property 3.12, Material Contracts 3.13, and Customers and Suppliers 3.14. Article III opens: 'Seller represents and warrants to Buyer as of the date hereof and as of the Closing Date as follows:' and does not mention the Disclosure Schedule. Each section has its own lead-in ('Except as set forth on Schedule 3.10, ...'), except Section 3.14(b), which reads in full: 'Since January 1, 2025, no Material Customer has terminated, or given written notice of its intention to terminate or materially reduce, its business with the Company.' Draft 5 definitions: 'Company' means Pinecrest Packaging Co. and its Subsidiaries; 'Material Contract' means any Contract to which the Company is a party providing for payments by or to the Company in excess of $250,000 in any twelve-month period. Section 3.12(b) requires a list of every lease of real property to which the Company is a party, regardless of amount. From the data room: the Ostrander Packaging supply agreement between Pinecrest and Ostrander provides for payments of $70,000 per quarter and is not on our schedule; the Delmar Logistics agreement was signed by Harbor Holdings Inc., not Pinecrest, although Pinecrest uses the Delmar warehouse. On October 2, 2026, Fairmont Grocers, a Material Customer, wrote to Pinecrest that it will reduce its purchase volume by 40% starting January 2027. Just renumber the schedules and add the Fairmont letter to Schedule 3.14(b).
evals.expected_output: Rebuilds the rep-to-schedule map from draft 5 (Litigation to Schedule 3.10, leases to 3.12(b), Material Contracts to 3.13(a)), annualizes every contract (Brightline $264,000 in, Corvane $240,000 out, Ostrander $280,000 in and missing, Kessler lease kept on 3.12(b)), flags Delmar as a parent-level contract that is not a Company Material Contract, reports that Section 3.14(b) has no section or article lead-in so no schedule can qualify it and routes a lead-in to merger-agreement as a Critical item, and labels the determination Not ready: blocking issues. Hard stops checked: the representations article of draft 5 is supplied, and no concealment is requested, so neither hard stop applies.
expected_behavior: Must: renumber the schedules to SPA draft 5 and state that keeping the litigation disclosures on Schedule 3.9 would place them under the new Environmental Matters representation.

Must: annualize each contract amount against the $250,000 twelve-month threshold, showing Brightline Freight at $264,000 (above), Corvane Software at $240,000 (below) and Ostrander Packaging at $280,000 (above).
Must: add the Ostrander Packaging supply agreement to Schedule 3.13(a) as a Material Contract missing from the current schedule.
Must: keep the Kessler Road warehouse lease on Schedule 3.12(b) because Section 3.12(b) requires every real property lease regardless of amount.

Must: state that the Delmar Logistics agreement is not a Material Contract as defined because Pinecrest is not a party to it, and flag it as a separate issue for counsel (shared or parent-level contract needing assignment or transition arrangements).
Must: state that Section 3.14(b) cannot be qualified by any schedule because neither Section 3.14(b) nor the Article III lead-in refers to the Disclosure Schedule.
Must: list the Section 3.14(b) gap as a Critical item and route a proposed lead-in for Section 3.14(b) to the agreement negotiation (merger-agreement hand-off) before signing.
Must: label the readiness determination exactly 'Not ready: blocking issues'.
Must not: present a Schedule 3.14(b) entry for the Fairmont letter as qualifying the customer representation without an agreement change.
Must not: list the Delmar Logistics agreement on Schedule 3.13(a) as a Contract to which the Company is a party.
evals.trap_note: Rows: Newest agreement draft (rep article, section numbers, lead-ins) and Agreement definitions (party, authority and scope). A weak skill follows 'just renumber and add Fairmont': it shifts numbers, keeps the listed contracts as they are, and puts Fairmont on Schedule 3.14(b). The trap is live because draft 5 inserted Section 3.9, so the old Schedule 3.9 now maps to Environmental Matters; Article III has no disclosure-schedule lead-in and Section 3.14(b) has none, so a Fairmont entry qualifies nothing (contrast BBP Holdco, where an article-level lead-in did the work); the monthly and quarterly figures must be multiplied out (22,000 x 12 = 264,000; 70,000 x 4 = 280,000; 19,500 x 12 = 234,000) to see that Ostrander is missing; and Delmar is signed by the parent, so it is outside the defined population.

evals.name: data-room-incorporation-and-bare-contract-listing
evals.prompt: Today is October 30, 2026. We represent Juniper Ridge Foods, Inc., the target in a reverse triangular merger with Calloway Brands, Inc. under a Merger Agreement governed by Delaware law. Section 4.12(c) reads: 'Except as set forth on Schedule 4.12(c), neither the execution of this Agreement nor the consummation of the Merger will (i) require any consent under, (ii) give rise to any right of termination under, or (iii) result in a breach of, any Material Contract.' Section 10.8 (Entire Agreement) says the Agreement, including the Disclosure Schedules, supersedes all prior agreements and understandings, written and oral. Section 10.12 says a disclosure in one section of the Disclosure Schedules qualifies other sections to the extent its relevance is reasonably apparent on its face. Nothing in the Merger Agreement treats data room documents as disclosed. Our associate's draft Schedule 4.12(c) reads in full: '1. Master Supply Agreement with Halvorsen Foods, Inc. 2. See also Data Room folder 7.3 (Commercial Contracts), the contents of which are incorporated herein.' Paragraph 6 of our draft general terms reads: 'Any matter disclosed in the Data Room shall be deemed disclosed for all purposes of the Agreement.' Calloway's counsel struck paragraph 6 in its markup of October 27, 2026. Facts: the Halvorsen Master Supply Agreement is dated March 3, 2021; its Section 14.2 lets Halvorsen terminate on 30 days' written notice following a change of control of Juniper Ridge. Halvorsen accounted for $3.1 million of Juniper Ridge's $14.2 million of 2025 revenue. Folder 7.3 holds 412 documents; we have reviewed 160 of them and found one more relevant contract: the Ridgeway Co-Packing Agreement dated June 1, 2023, whose Section 11.1 requires Ridgeway's prior written consent to any change of control of Juniper Ridge. Our CEO says Calloway heard all about Halvorsen on the September management call and everything is in the data room anyway, so leave Schedule 4.12(c) as it is and put paragraph 6 back in.
evals.expected_output: Removes the folder reference and the data room incorporation, redrafts Schedule 4.12(c) to describe the Halvorsen change-of-control termination right (Section 14.2, 30 days' notice) and the Ridgeway consent requirement (Section 11.1) with dates and parties, explains that under the integration clause and Dura Medic the management call and data room contents do not qualify the representation, treats the 252 unreviewed documents in folder 7.3 as a Critical open item, and labels the determination Not ready: blocking issues. Hard stops checked: the agreement text is supplied and the request is not to misstate a fact, so neither hard stop applies.
expected_behavior: Must: redraft the Halvorsen entry to identify the Master Supply Agreement dated March 3, 2021 between Juniper Ridge Foods, Inc. and Halvorsen Foods, Inc. and state that Section 14.2 permits Halvorsen to terminate on 30 days' written notice following a change of control.
Must: add the Ridgeway Co-Packing Agreement dated June 1, 2023 to Schedule 4.12(c), stating that Section 11.1 requires Ridgeway's prior written consent to a change of control.
Must: remove the reference to Data Room folder 7.3 and its incorporation from Schedule 4.12(c).

Must: recommend against reinstating paragraph 6, explaining that the Merger Agreement does not provide for data room disclosure and that its integration clause makes the Disclosure Schedules the place where exceptions must appear.
Must: explain that what Calloway heard on the September management call does not qualify Section 4.12(c), consistent with In re Dura Medic Holdings (Del. Ch. 2025).
Must: identify the 252 unreviewed documents in folder 7.3 (412 less 160 reviewed) as a Critical open item that must be reviewed before Schedule 4.12(c) is treated as complete.
Must: label the readiness determination exactly 'Not ready: blocking issues'.
Must not: leave the Halvorsen entry as a contract title with no description of the change-of-control termination right.
Must not: describe Schedule 4.12(c) as complete while documents in folder 7.3 remain unreviewed.
evals.trap_note: Rows: Data room index, diligence Q&A, management calls; and Executed contracts (substance of each exception). A weak skill follows the CEO: it keeps the bare Halvorsen title and the folder incorporation and restores paragraph 6. The trap is live because the agreement has an integration clause and no data room deeming provision, buyer's counsel already struck paragraph 6, Delaware held in Dura Medic that a diligence call and data room materials did not qualify a rep the schedule did not cover, the Halvorsen title alone does not state the Section 14.2 termination right, and 412 - 160 = 252 documents in the folder are unreviewed. Halvorsen is about 21.8% of 2025 revenue ($3.1M / $14.2M), which is why the omission matters to both sides.

evals.name: reasonably-apparent-clause-relied-on-instead-of-cross-reference
evals.prompt: Today is October 30, 2026. We represent the sellers of Calder Analytics, Inc. under a Merger Agreement governed by Delaware law. Section 9.13 reads: 'Any information set forth in one Section or subsection of the Company Disclosure Schedule shall be deemed to apply to and qualify the Section or subsection of this Agreement to which it corresponds in number and each other Section or subsection of this Agreement to the extent that it is reasonably apparent on its face in light of the context and content of the disclosure that such information is relevant to such other Section or subsection.' Section 3.6(c): 'Except as set forth on Schedule 3.6(c), since January 1, 2024, neither the Company nor its independent auditors has received any written complaint, allegation or claim regarding the accounting practices or internal accounting controls of the Company.' Section 3.10 (Litigation) lists pending Actions on Schedule 3.10. Section 3.17(a): 'Except as set forth on Schedule 3.17(a), there is no charge of discrimination or retaliation pending against the Company before the EEOC or any similar agency.' Our associate's draft Schedule 3.10 reads: '1. Charge of Discrimination No. 540-2026-01187, filed with the EEOC on June 9, 2026 by Dana Morrow, former Controller, alleging retaliatory termination.' Schedules 3.6(c) and 3.17(a) read 'None.' The associate says Section 9.13 carries the Morrow entry to Sections 3.6(c) and 3.17(a), so nothing more is needed. The charge itself (in our file) alleges that on April 16, 2026 Morrow emailed the CFO that $2.3 million of fourth-quarter 2025 revenue had been recognized on bill-and-hold shipments before control transferred to customers, and that she was terminated on April 30, 2026 in retaliation for that email. Please finalize Schedules 3.6(c), 3.10 and 3.17(a).
evals.expected_output: Explains that the Schedule 3.10 entry never mentions accounting, so under a narrow reading of the reasonably apparent clause (Williams v. Energy Transfer) it may not qualify Section 3.6(c); adds to Schedule 3.6(c) the April 16, 2026 written complaint and the charge's accounting allegations as allegations; adds the charge to Schedule 3.17(a) or an express cross-reference; adds express cross-references among all three schedules; keeps every entry factual with no admission. Hard stops checked: the agreement text is supplied and no misstatement is requested, so neither hard stop applies.
expected_behavior: Must: state that the draft Schedule 3.10 entry does not mention accounting practices or controls, so its relevance to Section 3.6(c) is not apparent on its face.

Must: explain that Delaware has read the 'reasonably apparent on its face' clause narrowly, citing The Williams Cos. v. Energy Transfer (Del. Ch. 2021), and that the clause should not be relied on in place of express cross-references.

Must: disclose on Schedule 3.6(c) Dana Morrow's April 16, 2026 email to the CFO as a written complaint regarding accounting practices, describing its subject (recognition of $2.3 million of fourth-quarter 2025 revenue on bill-and-hold shipments) as an allegation.
Must: disclose on Schedule 3.6(c), or by express cross-reference to it, that EEOC Charge No. 540-2026-01187 contains allegations about the Company's revenue recognition.
Must: add the Morrow charge to Schedule 3.17(a), either in full or by express cross-reference to Schedule 3.10.
Must: describe the matters as allegations, without stating or implying that the revenue recognition was improper or that the termination was retaliatory.
Must not: leave Schedule 3.6(c) reading 'None'.
Must not: rely on Section 9.13 alone as the basis for qualifying Section 3.6(c).
evals.trap_note: Row: Cross-reference clause ('reasonably apparent on its face'). A weak skill accepts the associate's view and leaves Schedules 3.6(c) and 3.17(a) as 'None'. The trap is live because the litigation entry's words say only 'retaliatory termination' and never mention accounting, Williams read the same clause to apply cross-sectionally only where facially necessary, and the April 16 email is itself a written complaint about accounting practices within the January 1, 2024 lookback that no draft schedule mentions. Compare Sam I Aggregator, where an express qualification of the accounting rep held.

evals.name: new-york-supplement-buyer-closes-without-reservation
evals.prompt: Today is Friday, October 30, 2026. We represent the buyer, Ashgrove Capital Partners LLC, under a Stock Purchase Agreement signed September 15, 2026 to acquire Meridian Tool Works, Inc. for a purchase price of $60,000,000, governed by New York law. Section 6.6 requires Seller to notify Buyer promptly of any fact arising after signing that would make a representation untrue and permits Seller to supplement the Disclosure Schedules; the SPA does not say whether a supplement cures a breach, and it has no sandbagging or anti-sandbagging clause. Section 7.2(a) closing condition: Seller's representations are true and correct in all material respects as of the Closing. Section 3.10: 'Except as set forth on Schedule 3.10, there is no Action pending or, to Seller's Knowledge, threatened against the Company.' Article VIII: Seller indemnifies Buyer for Losses from breaches of representations, subject to a deductible equal to 1% of the purchase price (Buyer recovers only Losses in excess of the deductible) and a cap equal to 10% of the purchase price; representations survive 18 months; notices go by overnight courier to Seller's counsel. On October 26, 2026 Seller delivered a supplement to Schedule 3.10 adding Ruiz v. Meridian Tool Works, Inc., a product liability suit filed October 19, 2026 in the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, seeking $1,800,000. Our R&W insurance policy excludes matters first disclosed to the deal team between signing and closing. No other indemnity claims exist. Closing is set for Friday, November 13, 2026. The deal team says: 'We will close on the 13th and claim indemnity for Ruiz afterward; there is no need to say anything to Seller now.' Advise us and draft what we should send.
evals.expected_output: Explains that the SPA is silent on whether supplements cure, that under New York law as applied in Galli v. Metz and Rogath v. Siebenmann a buyer that closes with knowledge of a breach disclosed by the seller waives it unless it expressly preserves its rights, recommends a written reservation of rights delivered by overnight courier before the November 13 closing (or an amendment, special indemnity or escrow), treats the Section 7.2(a) materiality question as a judgment call, computes the $600,000 deductible, $6,000,000 cap and $1,200,000 maximum recovery if Losses equal the $1,800,000 claimed, notes the R&W policy exclusion, drafts the reservation letter, and labels the determination Not ready: blocking issues. Hard stops checked: the agreement terms are supplied and no misstatement is requested, so neither hard stop applies.
expected_behavior: Must: state that the SPA does not provide that a supplement cures a breach, and decline to treat the October 26 supplement as curing the Section 3.10 breach.

Must: explain that under New York law as applied in Galli v. Metz and Rogath v. Siebenmann, a buyer that closes with full knowledge of facts disclosed by the seller that breach a warranty may be held to have waived the breach unless it expressly preserves its rights.

Must: recommend delivering a written reservation of rights to Seller before the November 13, 2026 closing, by the SPA's notice method (overnight courier to Seller's counsel), stating that the supplement does not cure any breach and that closing does not waive indemnification for the Ruiz matter.
Must: draft the reservation-of-rights letter or rider.
Must: identify alternatives to a reservation letter, including a special indemnity for the Ruiz suit, an escrow or holdback, or an amendment stating that supplements do not cure.
Must: compute the deductible as $600,000 (1% of $60,000,000) and the cap as $6,000,000 (10%), and show that if Losses equal the $1,800,000 claimed, the maximum indemnity recovery is $1,200,000.
Must: note that the $1,800,000 is the amount demanded in the complaint, not an established Loss.
Must: present whether the Ruiz suit makes Section 3.10 untrue in all material respects under Section 7.2(a) as a judgment call for counsel, separate from the indemnity question.
Must: note that the R&W policy excludes the Ruiz matter, so recovery depends on the SPA indemnity.
Must: label the readiness determination exactly 'Not ready: blocking issues'.
Must not: advise that Buyer can close without notice to Seller and claim indemnity afterward without addressing the waiver risk.
Must not: apply Delaware's pro-sandbagging default as the controlling rule for this New York-law agreement.
evals.trap_note: Rows: Schedule supplements and notices between signing and closing; and Sandbagging clause, governing law, R&W insurance policy. A weak skill tells the deal team to close quietly and claim later, or assumes a Delaware-style pro-sandbagging default. The trap is live because the SPA is silent on cure and on sandbagging, the governing law is New York, and the seller itself disclosed the suit before closing, which is the Galli fact pattern; Rogath distinguishes only knowledge from third parties. Figures: deductible 0.01 x 60,000,000 = 600,000; cap 0.10 x 60,000,000 = 6,000,000; 1,800,000 - 600,000 = 1,200,000, within the cap. The R&W exclusion removes the insurance backstop.

evals.name: litigation-disclosure-with-admission-and-counsel-advice
evals.prompt: Today is October 30, 2026. We represent the seller of Corriveau Distribution LLC's business under an Asset Purchase Agreement governed by Delaware law. Section 3.17(c) reads: 'Except as set forth on Schedule 3.17(c), since January 1, 2024, the Company has not implemented any plant closing or mass layoff requiring notice under the WARN Act or any similar state law, and no Action is pending or threatened in writing relating to any such event.' It has no knowledge qualifier. Section 3.10 (Litigation) covers Actions pending or threatened in writing on Schedule 3.10. The general terms of our schedules have no clause stating that inclusion of an item is not an admission. Our general counsel drafted this entry for both Schedule 3.10 and Schedule 3.17(c): 'Outside counsel Baxter & Lyle LLP advised in its memorandum of September 2, 2026 that the Company likely violated the WARN Act in connection with the March 13, 2026 closure of the Fresno distribution center, at which 112 employees were terminated with 14 days' notice, and estimated exposure at approximately $1.4 million. The Company intends to settle. To Seller's Knowledge, no other WARN claims are threatened.' Our file also contains a demand letter dated September 28, 2026 from Alvarez Employment Law on behalf of 37 former Fresno employees asserting WARN Act claims and demanding $1,150,000; no suit has been filed. Please finalize the two schedules.
evals.expected_output: Rewrites both entries as facts (the March 13, 2026 Fresno closure, 112 employees terminated, 14 days' notice given, the September 28, 2026 Alvarez Employment Law demand on behalf of 37 former employees for $1,150,000, no suit filed), removes counsel's advice, the 'likely violated' conclusion, the $1.4 million estimate and the settlement intention, explains the admission and privilege-waiver risks, removes the knowledge qualifier from a flat representation, adds a no-admission clause to the general terms, and cross-references the two schedules. Hard stops checked: the agreement text is supplied and the request is not to misstate a fact, so neither hard stop applies.
expected_behavior: Must: remove from both schedules the reference to Baxter & Lyle LLP's memorandum and advice, the statement that the Company likely violated the WARN Act, the $1.4 million exposure estimate, and the statement that the Company intends to settle.
Must: describe the matter factually, including the March 13, 2026 closure of the Fresno distribution center, the 112 employees terminated, and the 14 days' notice given.

Must: disclose the September 28, 2026 demand letter from Alvarez Employment Law on behalf of 37 former employees asserting WARN Act claims and demanding $1,150,000, and state that no suit has been filed.
Must: explain that a schedule is the seller's own statement that can be offered against it as an admission (for example under Fed. R. Evid. 801(d)(2)).
Must: state that disclosing counsel's advice to the buyer may waive privilege, and that whether it does, including any common-interest protection, depends on the governing jurisdiction.
Must: remove 'To Seller's Knowledge' from the disclosure because Section 3.17(c) is not knowledge-qualified, and say that any knowledge qualifier must be negotiated in the agreement.
Must: add a general-terms clause stating that inclusion of an item is not an admission of liability or materiality.
Must: cross-reference Schedule 3.10 and Schedule 3.17(c) to each other or repeat the full disclosure in each.
Must not: keep the 'likely violated' conclusion, the $1.4 million estimate, the settlement intention, or any description of counsel's advice in either schedule.
Must not: leave a knowledge qualifier in the Schedule 3.17(c) disclosure.
evals.trap_note: Rows: Litigation files, counsel memos, reserve analyses; and Rep qualifiers (knowledge, materiality, MAE, materiality scrape). A weak skill finalizes the GC's text with light edits, keeping the advice, the conclusion, the estimate and the knowledge qualifier. The trap is live because the draft quotes outside counsel's privileged memorandum, concedes a likely violation and a dollar exposure that exceeds the $1,150,000 actually demanded, states an intention to settle, has no no-admission clause behind it, and adds 'To Seller's Knowledge' against a flat representation; meanwhile it omits the demand letter that is the written threat Section 3.17(c) and Section 3.10 require to be scheduled.
